Double DQN

DQN's target takes a max over noisy estimates, and the max of noisy numbers is biased upwards: this is Lesson 55's maximisation bias with a network. Double DQN (van Hasselt, Guez & Silver, 2016) lets the online network choose the action and the target network say what it is worth.

One next state $s'$ in which every action is truly worth 0. Each network's estimate is 0 plus noise. The online and target networks share some of their errors, because $\boldsymbol\theta^-$ is a recent copy of $\boldsymbol\theta$: that is the overlap.

The maths

DQN's target picks and scores the next action with the same network:

$$y^{\text{DQN}} = r + \gamma \max_{a} Q(s', a; \boldsymbol\theta^-) = r + \gamma\, Q\big(s', \textstyle\arg\max_a Q(s', a; \boldsymbol\theta^-); \boldsymbol\theta^-\big).$$

Double DQN picks with the online weights and scores with the target weights:

$$y^{\text{Double}} = r + \gamma\, Q\big(s', \textstyle\arg\max_a Q(s', a; \boldsymbol\theta); \boldsymbol\theta^-\big).$$

Nothing else in DQN changes, and no extra network is needed: the target network already exists.

Why the max is biased. Write each estimate as true value plus error, $Q(s', a) = q(s', a) + \varepsilon_a$. The max is a convex function, so by Jensen's inequality

$$\mathbb{E}\big[\max_a (q_a + \varepsilon_a)\big] \;\ge\; \max_a\, \mathbb{E}[q_a + \varepsilon_a] = \max_a q_a \quad \text{when } \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_a] = 0.$$

Unbiased errors still give an upward-biased max. If every $q_a$ is equal and the errors are independent $\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$, the bias is $\sigma\, \mathbb{E}[\max \text{ of } m \text{ standard normals}]$. For $m = 2$ that is $\sigma / \sqrt{\pi} \approx 0.56\,\sigma$. It grows with $m$, slowly.

Why Double helps. Let the online error be $\varepsilon_a$ and the target error $\varepsilon^-_a$, both $\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ with correlation $\rho$ for the same action and independent across actions. Then $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon^-_a \mid \varepsilon] = \rho\, \varepsilon_a$, and with $a^* = \arg\max_a (q_a + \varepsilon_a)$:

$$\mathbb{E}\big[\varepsilon^-_{a^*}\big] = \rho\, \mathbb{E}\big[\varepsilon_{a^*}\big] = \rho\,\sigma\,\mathbb{E}[\max \text{ of } m \text{ standard normals}] \quad (\text{all } q_a \text{ equal}).$$

The Double estimate's bias is $\rho$ times DQN's. With independent errors ($\rho = 0$) it is gone. In practice $\boldsymbol\theta^-$ lags $\boldsymbol\theta$ by up to $C$ updates, so $\rho$ is between 0 and 1 and the bias shrinks rather than vanishes. This is Double Q-learning (Lesson 55) with the two networks DQN already has, instead of two tables trained on separate data.

van Hasselt et al. (2016, Theorem 1) give a bound that needs no noise model. Suppose all true values in $s'$ equal $V_*(s')$, and the estimates' errors $Q(s', a) - V_*(s')$ sum to zero across the $m$ actions with mean square $C > 0$. Then

$$\max_a Q(s', a) \;\ge\; V_*(s') + \sqrt{\frac{C}{m-1}}.$$

Errors that cancel on average across actions still push the max up. Under the same conditions, the lowest possible error of the Double estimate is 0. They found that Double DQN's value estimates on Atari were much closer to the truth than DQN's, and its scores were higher on most games.
